opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's helpful to think of these tools as sitting on a spectrum. At one end you have something like CVC5, which is an SMT solver. It's a fully automatic engine: you hand it a logical formula, maybe about integers, bit vectors, arrays, strings, and it comes back and says "this is satisfiable, here's a model," or "this is unsatisfiable," meaning it's true in all cases. You don't interact with it, you don't guide it. It's fast, and it's become incredibly powerful over the last twenty years. But the intended audience isn't really the end user. It's tool builders. People like us, building systems on top of it, whether that's checking access control policies, network configurations, or the correctness of cryptographic code. CVC5 is the engine under the hood.

At the other end you have something like Lean, which is an interactive theorem prover. There, a human, often a mathematician or a very specialized engineer, is writing the proof step by step, and Lean checks every step against a small trusted kernel. It's extremely expressive. You can formalize pretty much all of mathematics in it, and the Mathlib community has shown that. But it takes real expertise, and historically it's been a fairly small audience: people with PhDs in this stuff, or mathematicians who've decided to invest the time.

What's exciting right now is that the line between those two is blurring. Interactive provers increasingly call out to automated solvers to discharge the boring subgoals, and now with large language models you have something that's actually pretty good at the creative, heuristic part, proposing the next tactic or lemma, while the prover gives you the guarantee that the result is actually correct. So the audience is expanding. What used to require a handful of experts can start to be used by ordinary developers, or even by people who just want to know that an answer to a question about, say, a policy is actually right, without ever seeing the logic underneath.

That's really the goal from my perspective: take this very deep, very rigorous technology and make it available to people who'd never call themselves formal methods experts, so that they get provable correctness as just a property of the system they're using.

r001.rationale: The response says CVC5 is aimed at tool builders and that Lean has historically served a small audience of experts and mathematicians.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating those two tools out a little bit, because they come from somewhat different traditions, even though they sit under the same umbrella of automated reasoning.

CVC5 is an SMT solver. You hand it a logical formula, often over theories like integers, bit-vectors, arrays, strings, and it tells you whether that formula is satisfiable, and if so, gives you a model. It's a workhorse. It's really designed to be a backend. The intended audience, honestly, isn't the end user. It's people building tools: verification frameworks, symbolic execution engines, program analyzers, policy checkers. At AWS, for instance, our customers don't really know that an SMT solver is running under the hood when they use something like IAM Access Analyzer. They just get an answer about whether a resource is reachable from the internet. The solver is the engine, not the car.

Lean is quite different. It's an interactive theorem prover and a dependently typed programming language. The audience there is much more hands-on. Mathematicians formalizing proofs, researchers who want very high assurance that a result is actually correct, and increasingly people building verified software where they want the proof and the program to be the same artifact. The trade-off is that Lean asks more of you. You're guiding the proof. You write tactics, you structure the argument, and the system checks every step. You get a tremendous amount of trust out of that, but it's a skill, and historically that's limited who could use it.

What's interesting to me right now is that the line between those two is getting blurrier. Lean has decision procedures and automation built in, some of which look a lot like what SMT solvers do. And on the other side, tools built on solvers are being pushed toward richer specifications where you'd previously have needed a proof assistant.

And then there's the bigger shift, which is that large language models are changing who the audience can be. A model can draft a Lean proof, or translate a plain-English policy into a formal query for a solver, and the automated reasoning tool acts as the ground truth that checks the model's work. So the capability of these tools hasn't fundamentally changed in the last couple of years, but the accessibility has. People who would never have learned the syntax of a theorem prover can now get the benefit of one, with the tool providing the guarantee that the model alone can't give you.

So my short view would be: CVC5 is infrastructure for tool builders, Lean is a precision instrument for people who need proofs they can fully trust, and both are becoming far more relevant to a general audience because of how well they pair with AI systems that are powerful but not inherently reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes CVC5 as infrastructure for tool builders and Lean as a hands-on tool for mathematicians and researchers, noting that Lean’s skill demands historically limited who could use it. This communicates that these tools traditionally served specialists.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish those two tools, because they ask different things of the user. CVC5 is an automated solver: you give it a logical formula, and it tries to determine whether that formula can be satisfied. You can use that to look for a counterexample to a claim about a system. Lean is an interactive theorem prover, where you express a theorem and construct a proof, with the tool checking the steps. There’s automation involved, but it’s a different style of interaction.

Both are very powerful, but that doesn’t mean they can take an arbitrary question and resolve it for you. Expressing the right question—making sure the mathematical statement actually captures what you care about—is a substantial part of the work.

The direct users tend to be people with some expertise in logic, mathematics, or formal verification. But I wouldn’t confuse the audience for the tool itself with the audience for its benefits. You can build a product that uses a solver underneath, where the user asks a question in the language of their problem and gets an answer they can act on. They don’t need to know which solver ran, or even that automated reasoning was involved. That’s a very important way to make these capabilities broadly useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the tools’ direct users tend to have expertise in logic, mathematics, or formal verification, clearly identifying them as specialist-oriented.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary tools. CVC5 is an automated solver: you give it a logical formula, and it tries to determine whether that formula is satisfiable. There’s a tremendous amount of sophistication behind that, but the experience can be very automatic within the theories it supports.

Lean is an interactive theorem prover. It gives you a language for stating mathematical claims and constructing proofs that a small kernel can check. There’s automation there, too, but you’re generally guiding the proof rather than just submitting a formula and waiting for an answer.

Historically, the direct users of these tools have been specialists—people working in verification, programming languages, or mathematics. But I think the audience for the capabilities is much broader. You shouldn’t have to become a logician to benefit from software that can establish whether a particular property holds. These tools can sit underneath interfaces that engineers already use, and AI can help translate between what a person wants to establish and the formal statement. The important thing is that the reasoning tool checks the result; we don’t have to rely solely on whether the AI’s explanation sounds convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says the tools’ direct users have historically been specialists, including people in verification, programming languages, and mathematics.
